1 Introduction Expertise in many professional domains is acquired through learning-by-doing: junior staff in law, medicine, science, engineering, and consulting master foundational skills while performing core job tasks under the supervision of senior practitioners. Such expertise has arguably become more, not less, necessary in the era of artificial intelligence (AI). Modern AI systems are easy to operate but hard to evaluate, so assessing their outputs demands the expert judgment that learning-by-doing instills. AI could strengthen this process or undermine it (Beane, 2024; Acemoglu et al., 2026; Afrouzi et al., 2026; Asriyan et al., 2026; Ide, 2026). It could accelerate the acquisition of expert judgment by supplying high-quality examples of professional work and on-the-spot feedback that managers might not provide and junior workers might hesitate to seek. Or it could stunt skill acquisition if junior workers offload tasks to algorithms and bypass the learning those tasks would otherwise generate, crowding out the judgment that effective AI use requires. 1 Evaluating AI tools in judgment-dependent tasks therefore requires more than measuring their impacts on short-term performance; it also requires quantifying how they affect skill acquisition. A growing body of evidence addresses the first question, demonstrating that AI boosts immediate performance and often narrows the gap between high and low performers (Noy and Zhang, 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Brynjolfsson et al., 2024; Cruces et al., 2026; Ju and Aral, 2025; Dell’Acqua et al., 2026). The skill acquisition question, however, remains underexplored. Answering it requires sustained AI use over an extended period, a measure of skill that is distinct from AI-assisted output, and experimental control over AI access. To our knowledge, no existing study combines all three in a high-stakes professional setting. We meet these requirements by evaluating the consequences of AI use among intellectual property lawyers, whose legal drafting work requires both technical precision and strategic judgment, and whose outputs are amenable to blinded expert evaluation. We partnered with eleven U.S. intellectual property law firms to conduct a three-month randomized controlled trial among 133 patent lawyers, 91 of whom completed the full protocol. All firms in the experiment have ongoing patent-drafting relationships with Google LLC, which facilitated recruitment, meaning that our sample best represents law firms that are sophisticated in patent law practice. Lawyers were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive access to a custom AI drafting assistant or to a no-AI control condition, with randomization stratified by firm and experience level. 2 All work products were scored by blinded patent attorneys at an independent law firm on a standardized rubric covering enforceability, accuracy, strategic ambiguity (the use of broad, flexible claim language that maximizes future enforcement scope within the USPTO’s “Broadest Reasonable Interpretation” standard), completeness, and clarity.
1 See e.g. Brynjolfsson et al. (2025); Hosseini and Lichtinger (2025); Modestino et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025) for evidence that AI diffusion is already leading to a decrease in junior-level hiring across sectors. Emanuel et al. (2026); Lambert and Schindler (2026) argue instead that the decline in junior hiring is better explained by the rise of remote work.
2 The 2:1 ratio balanced the research team’s preference for an even split against patent firms’ preference for giving more of their lawyers AI access sooner.
The trial comprised three assessments at two points in time. At 10 days, lawyers completed a patent-drafting task; at 90 days, they completed a second drafting task and an unassisted redlining task. The drafting tasks measure the immediate effect of AI on assisted performance. Because treatment and control face the same task in each wave, comparing the treatment-control gap at 10 days with the same gap at 90 days reveals whether performance differences widen or narrow with extended use. The redlining task instead measures professional judgment. Conducted ‘offline’, without AI, it asks lawyers to evaluate and mark up existing professional work, a task patent lawyers routinely perform unaided and one that foregrounds expert judgment rather than text production. Comparing the offline performance of lawyers immersed in AI-assisted drafting for three months against that of lawyers without AI access separates the skill lawyers have internalized from their AI-assisted performance.
3 Our central finding is that AI’s effects on output and on expertise diverge. Measured by output, access to AI improved the quality of lawyers’ patent drafts. Lawyers provided with AI access outperformed controls by 0.34 SD at 10 days ( 𝑝 = 0.03) and 0.38 SD at 90 days ( 𝑝 = 0.01). These gains are visible across all five scored domains, with larger point estimates for juniors than for seniors. Higher average scores reflect lower prevalence of weak work, not higher prevalence of excellent work. Measured by unassisted judgment, only senior lawyers emerged from three months of AI use with improved capability. In the unassisted redlining task, the treatment group outperformed the control group by 0.32 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.04). But this effect stems entirely from better redlining by senior lawyers. Junior lawyers in the treatment group show no average gain in redlining quality relative to controls. Moreover, their scores were more dispersed, with significantly fewer mediocre scores, significantly more poor scores, and an offsetting rise in good but not excellent scores. This pattern is consistent with AI accelerating skill acquisition among some juniors and substituting for it among others. Our experiment does not answer why the effects appear positive for some lawyers and negative for others. AI access also sped drafting. Treated lawyers spent about 10 fewer minutes on the 10-day drafting task than controls ( 𝑝 = 0.05), whose mean was 110 minutes, with similar but less precise savings at 90 days. Point estimates for time savings are substantially larger for junior than senior lawyers, though the contrast between these estimates is not statistically significant. Distinct from the patent drafting tasks, the treatment group realized no time savings relative to the control group in the unassisted redlining task. In both treatment and control groups, senior lawyers spend longer on average than juniors performing the redlining task, perhaps reflecting the expertise-intensive nature of this task.
3 Our interpretation of differences in endline performance in redlining as reflecting differences in skill acquisition relies on the assumption of treatment-control skill balance at baseline. The evidence reported below supports this assumption. (Our preferred research design had subjects performing both a baseline and an endline skills assessment, but this feature proved an impediment to recruiting firms to the study.)
2
Several analyses confirm the robustness of these results to measurement and inference choices. Treatment effects on assisted drafting and on unassisted redlining hold across all five scoring subscales, with senior redlining gains near-uniform across domains and junior gains absent in every one, though precision falls at the subscale level. Because each task is scored by at least two independent raters, we verify that the results are not driven by rater idiosyncrasies. Given the risk of poor standard error coverage in small samples, we also report a nonparametric permutation test that affirms the primary findings. Ratings by a Large Language Model corroborate the human raters on the overall drafting gains, though not consistently on whether juniors or seniors gain more. On redlining, LLM ratings yield a positive but insignificant estimate for treated juniors and a larger, significant one for treated seniors. We explore two concerns that apply to the central finding that senior but not junior lawyers gain in offline work. The first is the classification of seniority. Using thresholds from three to eleven years of experience, we find the same pattern: positive point estimates for assisted drafting in both groups at every threshold, and significant unassisted gains only among seniors. The second is that treated senior lawyers might have used AI on the redlining exercise itself. Using LLM evaluations and manual audits to flag textual tells of AI use, and erring toward over-classification, we identify 15 of 91 redlining submissions where AI use appears possible. Flagged submissions score insignificantly higher than unflagged submissions, and neither controlling for nor excluding them changes the inference for seniors. Excluding them lowers the full-sample estimate below conventional significance, while the senior effect remains significant at the 10 percent level. With LLM ratings, both estimates are larger and significant at the 1 percent level. Our findings point to a trade-off between immediate productivity gains and durable skill acquisition. Junior lawyers capture the largest immediate gains from AI use, paralleling evidence from writing (Noy and Zhang, 2023), customer service (Brynjolfsson et al., 2024), and software development (Ju and Aral, 2025). But on the unassisted redlining task, The skill gains from AI exposure accrue entirely to senior lawyers. Treated juniors perform no better on average than control juniors, and their scores bifurcate: more good and more poor scores with no gain at the top of the distribution. That the group gaining most in output gains nothing in measured expertise suggests that foundational expertise may be a prerequisite for converting AI assistance into durable learning. This tradeoff matters so long as professional work demands judgment exercised without AI. In the domain of law, we expect that to remain true indefinitely. AI may increasingly assist with tasks such as redlining, but it is far less able to help lawyers as they advise clients, negotiate with counterparties, or respond to a patent examiner in real time.
2 AI in professional services: Productivity and skill development Generative AI has diffused rapidly into knowledge work. Bick et al. (2026) report that 43% of US workers used generative AI for work in the first quarter of 2026, with adoption close to 60% 3
in business, management, and finance. Adoption in law is rising as well: the share of legal organizations actively using generative AI nearly doubled from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025, and 45% of law firms report either currently using or planning to make AI central to their workflow within a year (Thomson Reuters Institute, 2025). This uptake has proceeded despite distinctive obstacles: privileged client information limits what AI systems can access, high-stakes documents amplify the cost of AI-introduced errors (Charlotin, 2026; Robert, 2026), and AI’s time savings threaten the time-based revenue model on which most law firms depend (Rapoport and Tiano, 2025). Legal practice is a consequential setting for studying AI’s effects on productivity and learning. The profession combines high-stakes output, domain-specific expertise that typically takes many years to acquire, and an apprenticeship structure through which junior practitioners develop expert judgment (Remus and Levy, 2017). These features are especially pronounced in intellectual property law, the domain we study. The precise language of a patent claim determines its legal force, drafting defensible claims requires extensive supervised practice, and evaluating patent quality is itself an expert domain. The two subsections that follow review the evidence on contemporaneous productivity and then on skill development.
2.1 Productivity impacts of AI use Following the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, experimental studies found consistent productivity gains across white-collar occupations, from management consultants to call-center employees to freelancers (Noy and Zhang, 2023; Hui et al., 2023; Brynjolfsson et al., 2024; Dell’Acqua et al., 2026). A common finding is that AI narrows performance gaps between new and experienced workers, between average and high performers, and between generalists and domain experts (Noy and Zhang, 2023; Cruces et al., 2026; Shen and Tamkin, 2026). In law, Choi and Schwarcz (2025) report an “equalizing effect” among law students, with sharp gains for those at the bottom of the class and declines for those at the top. This leveling is not universal: in a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, Otis et al. (2026) find that an AI business mentor raised the performance of high performers while lowering that of low performers. The form of the gain varies. Among knowledge workers and trainees, some studies find speed gains (Dillon et al., 2025), others find quality gains (Ju and Aral, 2025), and some find both (Haslberger et al., 2025; Usdan et al., 2024). One explanation is that workers reallocate time savings into additional effort on the same task, so an underlying productivity gain surfaces as speed, quality, or both, depending on circumstances (Humlum and Vestergaard, 2025a). In some cases, AI fails to improve performance or erodes it. In an experiment with 227 professional radiologists, Agarwal et al. (2023) find that access to AI predictions does not raise diagnostic accuracy on average: clinicians underweight correct AI signals and treat their own judgment and AI output as statistically independent. Goh et al. (2024) report that physicians using GPT-4 perform no better than physicians using conventional diagnostic tools, even though GPT-4 alone 4
substantially outperforms both groups. Outside of medicine, Dell’Acqua et al. (2026) document that consultants working beyond the “jagged frontier” of AI capabilities produce worse outputs with AI than without it, as users fail to recognize when AI outputs are wrong. In a meta-analysis of 106 experiments and 370 effect sizes, Vaccaro et al. (2024) find that human-AI combinations on average perform worse than the better of human or AI alone, with shortfalls largest on decision tasks and when AI outperforms unaided humans. These findings suggest that gains from AI use may be conditional on users’ ability to evaluate, integrate, or override its outputs, a capacity that may demand domain expertise. Studies of AI in legal writing, the setting of our experiment, are mostly conducted with law students and measure contemporaneous output. Comparisons of human- and AI-generated legal text find AI output approaching and in many cases exceeding human quality (Wrzesniowska, 2023; Martin et al., 2024; Vals AI, 2025). Experiments that measure performance find that gains accrue mainly to speed. Choi et al. (2024) find that GPT-4 access produces large and consistent time savings across baseline performance levels but only slight and inconsistent quality improvements in legal analysis. Nielsen et al. (2024) find that AI-generated highlighting of relevant text cuts completion time by 30% with no measured quality loss, while AI summaries alone show no improvement. Schwarcz et al. (2026), using two “reasoning” models that generate intermediate steps before answering, find consistent quality improvements on five of six assignments completed by upper-level students. We are aware of one prior RCT with employed lawyers: Chien and Kim (2025) gave 91 legal aid lawyers AI access and randomly assigned 40% of them a broader set of tools and “concierge” support; in follow-up surveys, that subgroup self-reported higher productivity. Ours is the first study to measure skill acquisition, rather than contemporaneous productivity alone, and the first to do so with practicing lawyers rather than law students.
2.2 Professional skill development If AI compresses the distribution of performance during assisted work but leaves underlying capabilities unchanged or degraded, its long-term effects on professional human capital will diverge from its short-term effects on output. Evidence on this question is mixed. Shen and Tamkin (2026), in a randomized experiment with software engineers learning a new programming library, find that AI assistance impaired conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging. Wiles et al. (2024) find that generative AI acts as a “temporary exoskeleton” for management consultants on unfamiliar data science tasks: these gains do not persist when the tool is removed. Among practicing endoscopists, Budzyń et al. (2025) find that routine AI assistance is associated with deterioration of unassisted diagnostic skill. Other studies find the opposite. He et al. (2026) document that novice radiologists who train with predictive AI subsequently make more accurate independent diagnoses. Cruces et al. (2026) find that less-educated participants who used generative AI on business problem-solving tasks improved modestly on unassisted follow-up tasks, and Lira et al. (2025) find that job-seekers who 5
practiced writing cover letters with AI improved their independent writing more than those who practiced without it. In the study closest to ours in design, Bednar et al. (2026) find that law students exposed to AI in an initial phase outperformed controls on subsequent tasks where AI access was removed. One reading of these divergent results is that workflows requiring users to interpret, evaluate, or verify AI output build skill, while those permitting uncritical acceptance bypass the effort on which learning depends. The most direct evidence for this interpretation comes from Bastani et al. (2025), who randomize nearly 1,000 high school mathematics students to practice with or without GPT-4. Unconstrained access improves in-session performance but lowers subsequent unassisted exam scores. When the same model is reconfigured as a tutor that withholds answers and requires students to reason through problems, the harm disappears. He et al. (2026) find that radiologists’ unassisted gains are largest when AI is deployed during both training and practice. A related conce

rn is that AI may disrupt the apprenticeship through which expertise is transmitted. Drawing on field studies of robotic surgery and other technologically mediated work, Beane (2024) argues that tools which raise immediate productivity often sever the process by which skill passes from senior to junior practitioners. Theoretical work formalizes the tradeoff: automating entry-level tasks can raise current output while slowing the accumulation of expertise (Afrouzi et al., 2026; Asriyan et al., 2026; Ide, 2026). The consequences of AI use for skill formation therefore cannot be
inferred from contemporaneous output. They must be measured directly. The present study provides direct measurement. We assess how sustained AI use shapes quality, productivity, and, most centrally, the development of expert judgment, tracking practicing pro- fessionals over three months in a high-stakes domain and pairing their AI-assisted output with a separate unassisted task scored by independent expert raters. The design separates AI’s effect on performance from its effect on skill acquisition.
3 Experimental design
3.1 Sample selection We began with a sample of 24 intellectual property law firms that are engaged in regular, non- exclusive business with Google. Eleven firms agreed to participate in the experiment. Two cohorts from one firm, enrolled two months apart, are analyzed as separate firms, giving an analytic sample of 12 firm cohorts. Recruits ranged from 3 to 49 participants across firms. To ensure that the time demands of the experiment did not compete with other professional activities, participants were, with the consent of their employers, paid at their contractual hourly rate for the time spent on experimental tasks. Table 1 provides a summary of firm-level recruitment, randomization, and task completion statistics, as well as experience levels of participating lawyers. Random assignment was conducted within each firm, with two-thirds of participants assigned to 6
treatment (AI assistance) and one-third assigned to control (no AI assistance). Assignment was stratified on the legal experience of participants, using the median level of years of experience within each firm to differentiate senior from junior intellectual property lawyers. 4 Of the 156 intellectual property lawyers put forward by firms, 133 (85%) completed the onboarding requirements and were successfully randomized into the trial. Because strata within firms were small, realized assignment ratios deviate slightly from the 2:1 target: 90 (68%) of the enrolled sample was placed in the treatment group and 43 (32%) in the control group. Table A1 reports tests of experimental balance. We see no statistically significant differences between treatment and control subjects across the limited set of pre-treatment individual characteristics available, including years of experience in the legal profession, responsiveness to outreach emails (measured in days), self-reported confidence in ability to execute experimental tasks, and self- reported comprehension of study requirements.
5
3.2 Experimental protocol Subjects in the treatment group were provided access via a gated online platform to the AI tool, an unreleased product developed by Google Labs designed to assist writing in professional services settings. The tool integrated user-provided context, style guidance, and user-specified writing goals. Its main features are prompt-based text modification, feedback from multiple AI editorial personas, and rule-based review of documents for internal inconsistencies.
6 Control subjects in the experiment accessed standard legal tools during the 90-day experimental treatment window but were not given access to generative AI writing tools. While it is widely observed that individuals access generative AI tools to perform their work even when this is discouraged by their employers (Microsoft and LinkedIn, 2024; Humlum and Vestergaard, 2025b), this is much less likely in legal services, where AI usage is tightly controlled to enforce accuracy and protect confidentiality.
The experiment had three phases: Onboarding and training: All participants were offered optional, asynchronous AI training modules. Both the treatment and control groups received foundational instruction on AI basics, covering: (1) commonly used AI terms; (2) an introduction to LLMs; and (3) prompt engineering. Participants assigned to the treatment group gained access to the AI tool and to a second training

All materials remained accessible for reference throughout the study. 10-day assessment: Ten days after the treatment group gained access to the AI tool, all participants were assigned a patent drafting task. 7 Working from a patent document containing a main claim that describes the overall purpose of the invention, they were asked to produce five to seven dependent claims, which are subordinate to the main claim, along with a detailed description drawn from patent figures and mock-up notes attributed to the “inventor” and their “enterprise client team.” This format closely simulates real-world settings in which intellectual property lawyers are engaged by their clients. 3.3 Data and measurement Our primary outcome variables are subjects’ performance on the drafting and redlining tasks. All tasks were scored by two independent raters who were blind to treatment status and drawn at random from a pool of six raters at a contracted intellectual property law firm. Raters applied a rubric that was developed in collaboration with Google’s in-house counsel and is reproduced in Appendix Table A7. The rubric evaluates five core dimensions of patent draft quality: enforceability, accuracy, ambiguity, completeness, and clarity. As shown in Figure A1, the scores given by the two raters randomly assigned to each task are moderately correlated, with Pearson correlations of 0.59, 0.47, and 0.55 for the 10-day drafting, 90-day drafting, and 90-day redlining tasks respectively. 11 We also supplemented these professional evaluations with an LLM rater, discussed in Section 4.3. Each drafting task had two separately scored parts, the dependent claims and the detailed description, and two raters scored each part on the same five-dimension rubric. Averaging across parts within rater and dimension gives ten scores per participant for each drafting task (5 dimensions × 2 raters). The redlining task was a single exercise requiring no averaging, and it also yields ten scores per participant, two per dimension. Due to privacy agreements with participating law firms, the time that participants spent on experimental tasks could not be directly observed. We indirectly measure it in two ways. First, participants were instructed to run a stopwatch application while working and to record the elapsed

Where subjects supplied both measures, we average them. (All survey items used for analysis are reported in Section 3 of the Supplementary Materials.) We had also planned to apply the same scoring rubric to patent drafts that participating lawyers produced for Google under contract during the study period. Two features of the setting made this infeasible: such drafts were produced infrequently across our sample; and lawyers worked in teams, which precluded attributing a draft to an individual’s treatment assignment. In place of these scores, the 90-day survey asked subjects to report, for each patent they drafted in routine work for any client over the same period, its completion time, the rounds of internal feedback and review it required, and its perceived drafting difficulty. The post-task surveys also recorded participants’ perceptions of the tasks they had just completed. At both 10 and 90 days, Likert items asked how the task compared to their routine drafting in the time it required (‘speed’) and in the quality of the output (‘quality’), and how satisfied they were with the drafting experience overall (‘satisfaction’). We also fielded monthly surveys that tracked perceived changes in routine-work difficulty, speed, job satisfaction, and internal reviewer scrutiny, along with subjects’ use of generative AI tools outside of the specific AI tool we tested. These surveys allowed us to detect potential problems with satisfaction, contamination, or spillovers. To understand how experimentally induced variation in access to the AI tool interacted with subjects’ regular use of generative AI, we included the following question in each of the three monthly surveys: “Outside of [the AI tool], how would you describe your use of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude, or specialized AI tools for lawyers such as Harvey AI, Ironclad)?” Respondents chose among four answers: 1) no use in personal or work contexts; 2) use only in personal contexts; 3) occasional use for work-related tasks; and 4) regular use in professional work. In all three months of the experiment, roughly four in five respondents report either no work-related use (responses 1 or 2) or occasional work-related use (response 3), as shown in Figure A3. However, the fraction of treated respondents reporting regular work-related use (response 4) exceeds that among control respondents in every wave, and this contrast is marginally significant in month two and significant at the 5 percent level in month three. The gap is 6.8 percentage points in month one ( 𝑝 = 0.36) on a control base of 13.5 percent; 12.9 points in month two ( 𝑝 = 0.08) on a control base of 7.1 percent; and 17.3 points in month three ( 𝑝 = 0.05) on a control base of 5.6 percent. The successive widening of the gap reflects a decline in regular use among control respondents and a corresponding rise in their occasional use; the share of treated lawyers who report regular work-related use is roughly 20 percent across all three waves. Pooling across the three survey waves, regular work-related use is significantly higher among treated than control lawyers in the full sample and the senior subsample, and marginally so among juniors (see lower panels of Figure A3). In summary, regular work-related use of generative AI was uncommon among patent lawyers during our study period (May 2025 to February 2026), but access to the experimental tool led to 11

greater use of other AI tools in work-related tasks.

4 Primary results: AI-assisted drafting and AI-unassisted redlining This section reports the impacts of AI assistance on our primary outcomes: drafting quality at 10 and 90 days, and 90-day redlining quality. The treatment group was instructed to use AI on the drafting tasks; both groups were instructed to complete the redlining task without it. Table 2 summarizes these outcomes for the full sample and by experience subgroup, reporting the mean pooled across the five rubric dimensions and each dimension separately. Each dimension is standardized relative to the pooled control-group distribution (mean zero, standard deviation one), so full-sample treatment-group means read directly as effect sizes in standard deviations. 15 Control means within experience subgroups are not by construction zero, so subgroup effects must be read as treatment–control differences. Most of our main findings are apparent in these summary statistics; the regression tables that follow provide formal tests.

The bottom rows of Tables 3 and 4 report one-sided tests of how AI access affects the relationship between experience and performance. 16 Broadly, AI access reduces junior–senior performance deficits. As expected, untreated seniors outperform untreated juniors at both assessments, signif- icantly so at 90 days ( 𝑝 = 0.26 at 10 days and 𝑝 = 0.05 at 90 days against the null that untreated juniors perform at least as well). The estimated treatment effect of AI access is larger for juniors. Though this differential effect is not itself significant ( 𝑝 = 0.15 and 𝑝 = 0.17 ), it affects performance ordering. With AI access, juniors outperform untreated seniors at 10 days ( 𝑝 = 0.05 ), though not significantly at 90 days ( 𝑝 = 0.31 ). At 10 days, performance of treated juniors exceeds that of treated seniors, though not significantly ( 𝑝 = 0.19 ). At 90 days, treated seniors outperform treated juniors at the 10 percent level (𝑝 = 0.1 against the null that treated juniors perform at least as well). These gains in drafting performance stem from a reduction in the prevalence of low scores. The reduction holds at both 10 and 90 days and in every experience subgroup, though it is not always precisely estimated. (Throughout, we number quintiles from the top of the score distribution, so that the first quintile holds the highest scores and the fifth the lowest, and we label them top, good, middle, mediocre, and poor.) As Table 5 and the histograms in Figure 2 show, AI access lowers the share of fifth-quintile (poor) scores by 0.19 ( 𝑝 < 0.01 ) at 10 days and by a smaller and less precisely estimated 0.11 ( 𝑝 = 0.12) at 90 days. The decline is larger among juniors, whose share of fifth-quintile scores falls by 0.25 ( 𝑝 = 0.01) at 10 days and 0.13 ( 𝑝 = 0.38) at 90 days, than among seniors, whose share falls by 0.18 (𝑝 = 0.03) and 0.09 (𝑝 = 0.24), respectively. Among junior lawyers, the displaced mass in the bottom segments of the distribution is largely mirrored by increased mass in the first (top) quintile: the share of junior scores in the first quintile rises by 0.21 ( 𝑝 = 0.01) in the 10-day drafting task, and by a directionally consistent but statistically insignificant 0.12 ( 𝑝 = 0.15) in the 90-day drafting task. Among senior lawyers, the more modest reduction in the prevalence of fifth-quintile (poor) scores is offset by greater mass across most other segments of the distribution, particularly the third (middle) quintile for the 10-day task (0.12, 𝑝 = 0.04) and the second (good) quintile at 90 days (0.11, 𝑝 = 0.14), though the latter is less precisely estimated. This drop in the frequency of fifth-quintile (poor) scores tends to reduce performance variance among treated relative to control subjects. A Levene test finds that AI access significantly compresses performance variance on the 90-day drafting task, overall (Levene 𝑝 = 0.03 ) and among senior lawyers (Levene 𝑝 = 0.08 ). At 10 days, the test does not reject equal variances (Levene 𝑝 = 0.12 overall). 4.2 Performance in AI-unassisted patent redlining This section addresses the key question that motivates our experiment: does extended access (90 days) to AI assistance affect performance in professional work executed without AI? We answer this question by evaluating work quality in the 90-day AI-unassisted redlining task introduced above. Table 6 reports the main results. The first three columns of the table document an overall improvement in the quality of AI-unassisted redlining performed by lawyers in the treatment relative to the control group. Treated subjects outperform controls on the redlining task by 0.32 SD overall ( 𝑝 = 0.04 , column 2). As column 4 of the table reveals, however, this aggregate gain is driven entirely by senior lawyers, whose work quality improved by 0.45 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.02 ). By contrast, the point estimate for junior lawyers is essentially zero (-0.03 SD, 𝑝 = 0.89). The aggregate performance gain in AI-unassisted redlining holds across quality subscales for senior but not junior lawyers, as documented in the third panel of Figure 1. In the full sample, the treatment effects of AI access on redlining quality are positive across all five quality dimensions (enforceability, accuracy, ambiguity, completeness, and clarity) and statistically significant at 𝑝 ≤ 0.10 in three of five cases. Here too the effects come from senior lawyers: treated seniors outperform senior controls in all five quality dimensions, all significantly

4.3 Robustness of key results We probe the main results in five ways: supplementing expert ratings with LLM ratings, a nonparametric permutation test, dropping individual firms, varying the seniority threshold, and auditing for unauthorized AI use in the redlining task.
Using LLM evaluations to supplement human evaluations Our main analysis compares the impact of AI access on the quality of patent drafting and redlining at eleven law firms, as assessed by blinded patent attorneys at an independent firm using the rubric described above. To supplement these expert assessments, we re-scored every drafting and redlining submission with a large language model (Gemini 2.5-flash), supplying one prompt per task that contained a brief task summary and the same scoring rubric given to the human raters. (Section 3 of the Supplementary Materials provides the full prompts.) The summary of LLM ratings in Table A3 shows that they recover the same broad pattern of results as the human evaluations, but the treatment-control gaps they imply are systematically larger. In pooled scores, the LLM ratings place treated subjects 0.50 standard deviations above controls in 10-day drafting against 0.37 in the human ratings, 0.89 against 0.45 in 90-day drafting, and 0.60 against 0.26 in 90-day redlining. Within each evaluator, scores across the five rubric dimensions are highly correlated. Across all tasks and evaluator types, including pooled expert and LLM ratings, the minimum pairwise Pearson correlation between dimensions is 0.75. (Section 2 of the Supplementary Materials reports within-evaluator correlations among quality dimensions.) The correlation between LLM and expert ratings is much lower. Averaging across subscales and across the two expert evaluations for each 23
submission, the LLM-expert correlation is 𝑟 = 0.47 in the 10-day drafting task, 𝑟 = 0.19 in the 90-day drafting task, and 𝑟 = 0.14 in the 90-day redlining task, as Figure A2 shows. Columns 5 through 8 of each main results table (Tables 3, 4, and 6) incorporate the LLM evaluations. Columns 5 and 6 use LLM evaluations alone, while columns 7 and 8 pool human and LLM evaluations. Given the low LLM-expert correlations in the two 90-day tasks, we treat the LLM as a third, less reliable rater and focus on the pooled models, in which expert evaluations contribute two of every three observations while the LLM evaluation contributes the third. Pooling expert and LLM ratings leaves the pattern of results intact and generally reinforces earlier conclusions. In 10-day drafting, the main effect rises from 0.34 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.03 ) to 0.40 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.00 ), the junior effect from 0.58 to 0.74 SD, and the senior effect is unchanged at 0.23 SD. In 90-day drafting, the main effect rises from 0.38 to 0.55 SD. The junior estimate is little changed at 0.56 SD, while the senior estimate rises from 0.30 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.08 ) to 0.55 SD ( 𝑝 = 0.00 ). This is the one place where adding LLM ratings alters the pattern: in the pooled ratings, seniors and juniors receive a comparable boost at 90 days. In 90-day redlining, our key outcome, the main effect rises from 0.32 to 0.42 SD and the senior effect from 0.45 to 0.54 SD, while the junior estimate moves from -0.03 SD (𝑝 = 0.89) to 0.12 SD (𝑝 = 0.57) and remains indistinguishable from zero. On net, supplementing expert ratings with LLM ratings corroborates our key results, with the caveat that the LLM rater is likely less reliable than the lawyers contracted to provide the expert ratings.
Nonparametric test of redlining results The positive impact of AI access on senior but not junior performance in AI-unassisted redlining work is the most important and least expected finding in our study. Given the small senior and junior subsamples that support these findings, we further probe the robustness of our main inference by applying a nonparametric test of treatment-control differences. Following Holt and Sullivan (2023), we re-estimate the specifications of columns 2 and 4 of Table 6 on the disaggregated subscale ratings, then draw 2,000 Monte Carlo permutations of the treatment assignment to construct null distributions for the intent-to-treat effect. Figure 4 plots the resulting null distributions. The permutation exercise leaves the point estimates unchanged and alters only the inference; all reported permutation 𝑝-values are two-sided. For the full sample, the estimated treatment effect of 0.32 falls at the 97.1 percentile of the null distribution ( 𝑝 = 0.05 ). Among seniors, the estimated effect of 0.45 falls at the 98.7 percentile ( 𝑝 = 0.02 ). An effect of this magnitude is unlikely under the sharp null of no treatment effect, supporting the inference that AI access carried over to improved performance in the judgment- intensive, unassisted patent redlining task. The junior estimate is near zero, at -0.03, and sits at the 46.8 percentile ( 𝑝 = 0.93 ), near the center of its null distribution, so we cannot distinguish it from zero.

Potential contamination by unauthorized AI use Participants were instructed not to use AI tools in the redlining task, and this instruction was highlighted in both the task assignment email and the task materials. We could not enforce it directly, however, since end-user privacy commitments preclude observing individual tool use. If treated subjects used AI while redlining, our estimate of the effect of AI access on AI-unassisted performance would be contaminated. Three pieces of evidence suggest that non-adherence does not drive our results. As a starting point, we have a limited amount of direct evidence against non-adherence. One firm completed the redlining task in a session separate from the drafting task, and we observe no use of the AI tool’s redlining feature at that firm during the session. This check is narrow, however. Second, we audited the redlining submissions for textual signatures of AI use. We prompted NotebookLM, running Gemini 3.0 Pro, to compare each redlined submission with its unedited baseline draft and to flag signatures of machine authorship: full-paragraph rewrites in place of targeted line edits; criticism bracketed by strained praise, a softening pattern characteristic of instruction-tuned models; dense use of LLM-typical vocabulary (“furthermore,” “additionally,” “moreover,” “delves”); loss of structural context across patent sections; change-logs supplied in lieu of executed inline edits; excessively nested outlines in the free-form feedback; and theatrical over-commitment to a reviewing-partner persona. For juniors, the prompt added one marker: uniform edit density across sections, which is inconsistent with junior lawyers’ typically uneven allocation of time between the early and later sections of a document. Each flag required a confidence score and a verbatim supporting quotation. (Section 3 of the Supplementary Materials reproduces the prompt in full.) The research team also audited the submissions flagged by Gemini manually, confirming that flagged submissions indeed showed evidence of non-adherence.
